These findings characterize how observed extraction varies across sensitive-data frequencies, model families, and training mechanisms, and highlight substantial differences in extraction behavior across models. Code and data are publicly available.

title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems
text:
arXiv:2611.31582v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.

title: SecondChance: Benchmarking Reliable Error Recovery in AI Agents
text:
arXiv:2611.31586v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents make errors while they act, and their reliability depends on what they do afterwards. Existing recovery benchmarks mostly inject faults, involve no user and score whether the task is eventually completed, so they cannot show whether an agent undid its own silent error, told the user, or faced an error that could not be fixed. We introduce SecondChance, an error checkpoint dataset and evaluation harness that profiles and measures error-recovery behaviour of AI agents. The errors are natural: they come from agents' own task attempts in $\tau^2$-bench, BFCL and AppWorld. Different agents then resume from the same checkpoints under one of four conditions: no assistance, an error notice, the error location, or repair guidance. We measure error correction, task success, policy compliance, preservation of environment state, repair durability and cost. We evaluate 12 models under all four conditions in 5,760 continuations. Recovery is rare: across its environments, the best model completes only 16% of recoveries unaided and 27% with repair guidance. Correcting is not recovering: with repair guidance, Llama-3.3-70B corrects 26% of $\tau^2$ errors but completes none, and 40 of 84 successful AppWorld continuations leave the error in place. SecondChance exposes these differences that task success alone cannot capture.

title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
text:
arXiv:2611.31588v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. Project website: https://jmarangola.github.io/one-phase-visual-rl/

title: Spec$^2$R: Recovering Emergent Properties in Supervised Vision Transformers
text:
arXiv:2611.31589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved strong performance across computer vision tasks, but the quality of their learned representations differs drastically depending on the training paradigm. While self-supervised ViTs often demonstrate emergent properties, such as object-aligned patch representations and attention maps, supervised ViTs typically lack these properties, even when trained with strong data augmentations. Understanding the origin of this difference is important for explaining and controlling the object-level structure. To investigate it, we perform a spectral analysis of supervised and self-supervised models, and identify a key distinction: MLP layers in supervised ViTs introduce high-frequency variations into patch representations, disrupting their spatial organization. Motivated by this finding, we propose Spec$^2$R, a lightweight spectral regularization method that fine-tunes the MLP layers of pretrained supervised ViTs. Spec$^2$R recovers object-aligned patch representations and attention maps, while improving adversarial robustness and preserving competitive classification accuracy.

title: GoldiBench: Right Tools, Wrong Amount -- Benchmarking Agents on Effect Judgement in Professional Editing
text:
arXiv:2611.31590v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real editing requests describe a look, not the steps to reach it, so an agent that serves them must judge how much of each tool the look takes. Existing benchmarks do not measure this: their tasks either state the tools and values, or leave the amount open and are scored by VLM judges that pass more than half of half- and triple-strength results. We introduce GoldiBench, a benchmark of 500 editing tasks in five professional applications (darktable, RawTherapee, GIMP, Inkscape, Blender), solvable by writing a program or by operating the GUI. Each task pairs a START image with a TARGET rendered from a hidden program, so the amount is fixed by a known target; the agent's edit is re-rendered and compared with TARGET, and the same task is posed with the tools and values, the tools only, or the goal only, separating operation from effect judgement. Across 25 open, GUI and closed models, agents operate well (99-100% with programs from 4B up when told the values) but fall off a cliff when they must judge the amount: given only the tools, the best model passes 19% of the tasks with programs and 33% through the GUI, and scale does not close the gap. Manuals barely help; the measured TARGET-START difference more than doubles the pass rate, but the same difference shown as an image does not for open models. Allowed four renders, agents almost always stop after the first; forced to compare, the strong models double their pass rate. Agents know the tools, but neither read nor check the amount.

title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
text:
arXiv:2611.31595v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.

title: RePT: 3D Geometry Emerges from 2D Relational Pretraining
text:
arXiv:2611.31601v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.

title: Adapt, Label, Distill: Foundation-Model Supervision for Efficient Object Detection
text:
arXiv:2611.31604v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Object detectors often transfer poorly to specialized domains, where box annotations are scarce and deployment requires compact, real-time models. Large vision foundation models can provide offline supervision, but their zero-shot predictions may be poorly aligned with the target domain. We present an adapt-label-distill pipeline that uses limited target annotations to specialize a foundation teacher and transfer its supervision to compact detectors. We adapt SAM3 on the labeled subset, generate pseudo-labels for the remaining unlabeled images, and train YOLOv11 students with confidence-guided supervision. Teacher confidence weights pseudo-label losses, while zero-gating retains uncertain hypotheses during assignment without applying their associated training losses. Experiments across six target domains and three student capacities show substantial gains in several domains, while revealing limited or negative transfer in others. Teacher comparisons under a common hard-label training recipe support the choice of SAM3, and comparisons with an EfficientTeacher adaptation provide additional evidence against an online SSOD baseline. With YOLOv11m, our pipeline improves over STAC-style self-training by up to 15.3 AP and reaches 51.6 AP on Garbage, compared with 54.1 under full supervision. On NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the deployed student achieves 188 FPS versus 2.9 FPS for SAM3, benefiting from foundation-model supervision without incurring the teacher's deployment cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zk2172-columbia/ProjectAdaptLabelDistill_ObjectDetection.

title: Noise-Level Adjacency in Diffusion Training
text:
arXiv:2611.31605v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models train one network across all noise levels, although their training objective is pointwise in the noise level. If training on each pair of adjacent levels were an independent problem, separate networks with the same total parameter count would be expected to match one shared network. But in practice, on images, sharing weights across levels gives better results, which hints at an implicit dependence on their order. An order fixes both which levels are adjacent and the direction in which they run. In this paper, we show that, of the two, the benefit of sharing rests on adjacency in the noise-level embedding. The fitting error of a shared network is bounded below by the distances between neighbouring posterior means, minus the change the network can make between neighbouring embeddings. We first distinguish adjacency from direction: on a Gaussian mixture and CIFAR-10, reversing the embeddings keeps every neighbour and leaves the fitting error unchanged, whereas shuffling them raises it. Second, we rule out sharing between distant levels as the source of the benefit: separate networks on contiguous ranges match the shared network at its width, and with the parameters fixed, breaking adjacency at the same places costs less than 40\% of a full shuffle. Dividing the levels at equal shares of these distances lowers the error of all but the smallest networks. We therefore show that the order of the noise levels enters a diffusion model through adjacency, with its direction being a design choice. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/Noise-Level-Adjacency-in-Diffusion-Training.

title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
text:
arXiv:2611.31608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.

title: Monitorable-by-design architectures for a post-Astra world: a compartmentalization-based approach
text:
arXiv:2611.31610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use, especially in combination with dangerous reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use, can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought in a way that might outlast monitorable chain of thought. We propose several variants of this architecture designed to balance tradeoffs and discuss other benefits, such as capability removal.

title: Multi-agent System for Automatic Discovery of Pareto-optimal Meta-solvers for PDEs
text:
arXiv:2611.31611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing linear solvers for discretized partial differential equations requires problem-specific expertise. We present a multi-agent framework, in which language-model agents propose, critique, implement, and evaluate solver configurations assembled from Krylov methods, preconditioners, block factorizations, and neural operators. Inside the proposing agent, a non-dominated sorting genetic evolutionary algorithm evolves the population of meta-solvers toward the Pareto front of six measured quantities, so that one run returns a front of trade-offs rather than a single tuned solver. The system runs on small open-weight language models served on a single laptop, and we compare it with a single agent on four problems. For three-dimensional acoustic scattering and elasticity, it delivers 47 and 48 convergent hybrid solvers out of 60 candidates. Relative to the Jacobi-preconditioned Krylov baselines, the best of the discovered solvers reduce the iteration counts by factors of 4.7 and 60 and the online solve time by factors of 2.3 and 3.0, whereas the single agent produces no executable plan. For coupled dynamic thermoelasticity in two and three dimensions, where the baselines fail, it completes 98 of 100 transient candidates and, compared with the single agent, reaches a given accuracy 15 times faster in two dimensions and a displacement error 20 times lower in three dimensions.

title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
text:
arXiv:2611.31613v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.

title: Tablassert: Declarative Extraction of Knowledge Graphs from Biomedical Tables
text:
arXiv:2611.31614v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tables published in biomedical research papers, particularly supplemental tables, capture knowledge assertions that may not be in the main text of the manuscript for several reasons, including low statistical significance, space limitations, and narrative scope. These tables include data (e.g., association statistics, assay readouts, curated gene lists, and omics) encoding relationships between biological entities. Tablassert converts such tabular data (Excel, CSV, TSV, Parquet) into knowledge graphs ready for the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator (Fecho et al. 2025). A user declares in YAML how each table's data map to subject-predicate-object-qualifier statements; Tablassert resolves free text (e.g., ''lung cancer'') to standard identifiers, attaches provenance and statistics, and emits graph files conforming to Translator standards (D. Unni, Bruskiewich, and Moxon 2026; D. R. Unni et al. 2022).

title: Eliciting sandbagged LLM capability via structural interventions on attention-head functional networks
text:
arXiv:2611.31615v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.

title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
text:
arXiv:2611.31619v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

title: Self-Improving Long-Horizon Reasoning by Learning Summaries from Local Continuations
text:
arXiv:2611.31621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.

title: What You See Is What You Certify: Concept-Based Certificates for Unseen Compositions
text:
arXiv:2611.31627v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Concept-based models justify a decision by concepts they claim to see, decoded through an explicit ontology. Yet concept predictions are known to leak label information, ignore locality, and be poorly grounded on new attribute combinations. A decision decoded from such concepts can satisfy the ontology and still be wrong, so we ask when it can serve as a certificate. On unseen combinations of familiar parts, a joint concept bottleneck model and a concept embedding model, trained as is standard, certify wrong classes 93-94% of the time despite a correct ontology (60% for a joint model trained only on visible parts and gated by a localizer). The joint model's part errors copy co-occurring values more often than chance (cross-concept shortcutting). Treating the ontology as an error-detecting code, we show that a certificate needs visible evidence excluding every rival, unseen parts reported as such, and rare misreads not driven by a shared shortcut. A minimal reference design, OCVE, reads each part from a local crop in its own forward pass. On unseen FunnyBirds classes, it certifies 52% of images at 0.4% risk, against 14% for mask-pooled features and 33% for full-image part readers (5.6% when trained and gated alike), at similar zero-shot accuracy. The best baselines, even calibrated or restricted to unseen classes, and a decoder counting only agreeing parts remain about 3-8 times riskier. On CUB, isolated region readers are more accurate than an attribute-prototype model (63.1% vs. 55.3%) and certify unseen species at about 6 points less risk than it and about 10 points less than features pooled in the same keypoint boxes. On real traffic signs, isolated readers lower certified risk from 99.8% to 67%, which is still far too high; most remaining errors are misread pictograms. On seen classes the ontology brings no gain over a fairly trained black box, and isolation costs accuracy.

title: Wavefront: Low-Rank Drafting with Parallel Causal Refinement for Speculative Decoding
text:
arXiv:2611.31638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.

title: Reward Basis Decomposition for Interpreting Preference Heterogeneity
text:
arXiv:2611.31640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Canonical reward models specify the optimization target for AI policies, so understanding the values they encode is important for ensuring AI alignment. Existing interpretability techniques interpret reward models with a single reward head, which cannot distinguish between the values that a population shares and those that vary among individuals. We introduce Reward Basis Decomposition (RBD), which splits per-user weights into a population term and a per-user term. This yields a shared population direction and individual user directions that are analyzed separately via concept alignment and sparse autoencoder decomposition. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. In both, we find no individual-user structure, suggesting that a single direction in the reward embedding space accounts for most preferences. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. In both, we find no reliable predictive benefit from the fitted per-user terms beyond the shared population direction under our setup. Code and the synthetic dataset are available at https://github.com/RachelFreedman/RBD.

title: E2SIM: Long-Horizon Simulation of Everyday Human Behavior with Evolving States
text:
arXiv:2611.31641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to support users over long periods, across work, and daily life. This requires modeling not only who users are, but also how their goals, interests, activities, and interactions evolve over time. A challenge in longitudinal user simulation is maintaining consistency between these evolving states and the consequences of actions in a shared environment. We introduce E2SIM, a longitudinal user simulation framework that jointly models evolving actor states and a dynamic shared environment. E2SIM connects actor-state updates with shared-world changes through a feedback loop linking immediate actions, delayed outcomes, and actor-specific observations across work and life. This allows the consequences of earlier actions to shape later behavior, while preserving differences in what each actor knows. We further propose a suite of longitudinal trajectory diagnostics, measuring dynamic consistency, coherent event progression and collaboration, and non-degenerate trajectory development rather than static consistency alone. In one 60-day simulation, E2SIM produced more extracted event threads judged meaningful by our evaluator and fewer near-duplicate actions than four direct-generation baselines. The framework and evaluation methods provide a basis for studying longitudinal user simulation, with potential applications in training and evaluating AI agents that assist users over extended periods.

title: MSW: a Multi-Scale Sliced Wasserstein Distance Between Image Distributions
text:
arXiv:2611.31647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose the multi-scale sliced Wasserstein (MSW) distance between image distributions, which operates in pixel space and requires no trained network. MSW convolves images with a fixed bank of discrete cosine filters at several scales, pools the responses over all positions, and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions using the Wasserstein distance. We pair MSW with an exact two-sample test that gives calibrated p-values. Most metrics compare two image sets in the latent space of a pretrained network. We show that these metrics are insensitive to simple perturbations of the images, because the latent space is nearly invariant to them. In contrast, MSW detects smaller perturbations than latent-space metrics and needs far fewer images to do so. Although it uses no learned features, it still detects semantic changes of the image distribution. Finally, MSW matches or outperforms existing Wasserstein-based metrics in our experiments.

title: Anchoring VAE Fine-Tuning to Its Latent Diffusion Prior
text:
arXiv:2611.31651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained latent diffusion models are effective priors for transfer learning, from geometry estimation to physics simulation. Existing approaches fine-tune the diffusion backbone but freeze the encoder of the VAE to preserve the latent distribution. However, a frozen encoder may miss salient details in non-RGB inputs and is limited to three channels. We introduce Diffusion Prior Anchoring (DPA), a regularizer applied during VAE fine-tuning that uses a score-distillation update to steer latents toward the high-density manifold on which the pretrained diffusion model denoises accurately. We validate DPA across three image and video models (FLUX 3, LTX-Video, Wan2.2) and four tasks: monocular depth estimation, MRI reconstruction, wind-flow simulation, and surface normal estimation, where DPA lowers the prediction error by 7.5% relative to the frozen VAE, 4.9% to decoder-only fine-tuning, and 4.0% to unanchored VAE fine-tuning. Its gain grows the further the target data lies from the RGB training distribution, from 3.3% on monocular depth estimation to 7.2% on complex-valued MRI. DPA also applies to modified VAEs, including pruned and multi-channel variants. With a four-channel VAE that encodes depth and surface normals, it lowers depth estimation error by 9.3%.

title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence
text:
arXiv:2611.31653v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.

title: Stranded Compute in AI Inference Workloads: Recovering Value Through Demand Aggregation
text:
arXiv:2611.31654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI inference infrastructure is commonly analyzed as an energy business. Under full total cost accounting it is not: in the reference deployment modeled here, capital recovery is 87.3% of fully loaded cost per token and electricity 3.7%. Because capital accrues per unit time irrespective of use, accelerator value is destroyed by non-utilization rather than by consumption. Yet, SLO qualified goodput reaches only 59.6% of nameplate throughput, and the decomposition of the loss chain shows that 25.2 of the 40.4 lost percentage points arise from scheduling idleness and stranded burst reserve. Both are properties of a tenant's demand portfolio rather than of its silicon, and neither is diversifiable by a single tenant acting alone. Modelling reserve and idle capacity as diversifiable risk, pooling demand across eight imperfectly correlated tenants (rho = 0.3) recovers 7.3 pp of goodput, approximately $0.75M per annum per megawatt of IT capacity, or between 2.8x and 4.9x the entire annual interconnection spend of the deployment that produced it. The implication for neutral colocation and interconnection providers is that the switching and interconnection layer aggregating tenant demand functions as an instrument of capital productivity while being priced as transport.

title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
text:
arXiv:2611.31656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.

title: Boundary Representation-Driven Graph Transformer Modeling for Machining Operation Sequencing
text:
arXiv:2611.31661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machining process planning is inherently complex due to the interdependence between part geometry, machining operations, and evolving manufacturable states. Traditional approaches rely heavily on expert knowledge and rule-based systems, limiting scalability and automation. While recent machine learning methods have shown promise, most operate on simplified geometric representations, such as voxels or hand-crafted features, which fail to fully exploit the rich geometric and topological information encoded in Boundary Representation (B-Rep) models. In this work, we propose a graph transformer-based framework for geometry-to-sequence learning that directly predicts machining operation sequences from B-Rep design geometry. The proposed method constructs topology-aware graphs from B-Rep entities, where faces and their adjacencies are encoded as node and edge features capturing both geometric and relational information. A graph neural network encoder learns geometry-aware embeddings, which are then used to condition a dual-decoder transformer that autoregressively generates machining operation sequences. This formulation enables the model to capture both operation-type prediction and process-level ordering constraints directly from design geometry, without requiring intermediate feature extraction or machining-state representations. Experiments on a dataset of 2,991 synthetic machined parts demonstrate strong performance, achieving 95% accuracy for main operation prediction, 64% accuracy for sub-operation prediction, and 93% accuracy for sequence length prediction. Further analysis shows that the model effectively captures precedence relationships and geometry-dependent constraints inherent in machining processes. These results highlight the potential of B-Rep-driven graph learning for scalable and automated machining process planning.

title: LineEX: Data Extraction from Scientific Line Charts
text:
arXiv:2611.31664v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we introduce LINEEX that extracts data from scientific line charts. We adapt existing vision transformers and pose detection methods and showcase significant performance gains over existing SOTA baselines. We also propose a new loss function and present its effectiveness against existing loss functions. In addition, we synthetically created the largest line chart dataset comprising 430K images. The code is available at https://github.com/Shiva-sankaran/LineEX.

title: A Piecewise-Linear Activation Function for Implicit Neural Representations
text:
arXiv:2611.31666v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coordinate networks with ReLU activations perform poorly on implicit neural representation tasks, and the activations that address this, such as sinusoids and Gabor wavelets, all leave the piecewise-linear function class, so it remains unclear which property of ReLU is at fault. We introduce JaSIN, a family of bounded piecewise-linear activations that interpolates between ReLU and a piecewise-linear sinusoid without any the use of transcendental operation. Our results show that a bounded range improves image reconstruction PSNR on average by 0.06 dB, a single bump 3.29 dB, and centering that bump a further 3.64 dB. The oscillation count improves 6.30 dB more, raising ReLU from 24.0 to 37.3 dB on Kodak images, placing third over eleven activations, within 1.3 dB of the state-of-the-art, though beyond four oscillations the reconstruction collapses. Because an INR is fit on the grid on which it is evaluated, a unit whose pre-activations never reach the support of its activation is certifiably inactive over the entire domain; deleting such units is lossless without fine-tuning, removing up to 84% of parameters at zero loss in performance (dB) and decoding 3.2 times faster. Reference code and demos are available at https://github.com/jeovafarias/jasin.

title: Provenance Loss and Repair in Multilingual Compaction
text:
arXiv:2611.31668v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversational assistants compact older messages into short notes and evict the originals. When the note's language requires a distinction that English leaves open, such as Spanish adjective gender (agotado vs. agotada), messages that omit or explicitly state that attribute can yield the same note. After eviction, later turns cannot tell them apart: taking the inflected form literally asserts an attribute the user never gave, whereas discounting it as routine grammar discards one the user did give. We propose a training-free repair across writing, pre-eviction verification and reading. The writer marks unstated attributes with paired forms (e.g., agotado/a), a likelihood check before eviction rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones, and the reader trusts remaining single forms as stated facts. On five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models, eviction cuts recall of stated attributes from 90% to 34% in question answering (QA); our repair raises F1 (which penalizes both errors) on every model, by 9-53 points in QA and 12-40 points in agent handovers.

title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training
text:
arXiv:2611.31670v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.

title: Medical Image Segmentation Is Now Just Another Coding Task
text:
arXiv:2611.31673v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For decades, every new medical image segmentation task has needed an expert, a dedicated architecture, and a framework such as nnU-Net. This is no longer the case: medical image segmentation is now just another coding task. Given only a task description, labeled data, and a CPU (with no segmentation framework, no pretrained weights, and no human in the loop), four off-the-shelf coding agents built segmenters for 13 tasks across four imaging modalities within hours, an ability that has emerged rather than been built. On the nine 2D tasks, their best programs reach 99% of the Dice of a GPU-trained nnU-Net. Like any code, a segmenter improves by being revised and checked, so we ask how far the same agents can improve their own segmentations and what unlocks further gains. On unseen cases there is no reference, so the agents inspect renderings of their own predictions: this alone lifts the worst tenth of cases by 0.09 Dice and cuts boundary error (HD95) by almost a quarter. Far more is within reach. Told the true Dice of each attempt, the same agents improve in all 14 matched pairs, rescue 85% of failed masks instead of 30%, and surpass the GPU-trained nnU-Net on average, by producing better masks rather than by choosing among them. What unlocks these gains is a quality signal, which neither visual inspection, nor more rounds, nor a quality estimator trained by the agents themselves yet supplies: we call this the quality blind spot. The ability to build and to repair is already present; the next advance will come not from another segmentation model, but from reference-free quality estimation that coding agents can call.

title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
text:
arXiv:2611.31677v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.

title: Curvature-Equilibrated Policy Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning
text:
arXiv:2611.31680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gradient-based actor optimization is central to deep reinforcement learning. However, conventional first-order optimizers do not explicitly exploit the local curvature of neural actor losses. We propose EQUIP (Curvature-Equilibrated Gradients for Policy Search), a novel approach that seeks to balance local contraction and expansion of the actor parameter space by equilibrating positive and negative curvature. EQUIP constructs a trajectory-informed search subspace and uses the projected Hessian of actor loss to build a bounded local metric for curvature equilibration. First-order loss matching preserves the approximated first-order decrease in actor loss. Meanwhile, gradient mixing and curvature-based gradient selection adjust the gradient applied for actor optimization. We establish the geometric properties of curvature equilibration, derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude, and identify conditions for improved actor loss reduction and convergence toward stationarity under direct gradient updates. We integrate EQUIP into Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) without modifying its actor loss, critic learning, or replay mechanism. Experiments on 6 MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks show that the resulting EQUIP-SAC algorithm achieves higher mean sample efficiency than SAC and two second-order policy optimization baselines. Ablation studies further highlight the benefits of curvature equilibration and trajectory-informed geometry for policy training.

title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
text:
arXiv:2611.31682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.

title: CROSS-Calib: Selective Channel Calibration for Ultrasound Reconstruction
text:
arXiv:2611.31684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ultrasound imaging provides views of internal tissue in real time for medical diagnosis. However, ultrasound signals may be affected by interference, and correcting errors and removing transient interference while preserving valid echoes remains challenging. We propose CROSS-Calib, a channel recovery method that uses predictions from other channels as references for amplitude and phase calibration, while a gate using context selectively combines calibrated measurements with predicted echoes to retain usable samples and repair unreliable ones. On the in vivo test set, CROSS-Calib outperforms all baseline models under gain errors and transient interference, while phantom tests show that the model restores cyst contrast with echo widths of wire targets close to the clean reference. CROSS-Calib can perform channel calibration and selective repair before beamforming to improve echo usability and image quality.

title: Right Destination, Wrong Journey: Synthetic Counseling Dialogues Miss Human Interactional Dynamics
text:
arXiv:2611.31686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-generated counseling dialogues are increasingly used for training and evaluating mental-health systems, yet existing evaluations focus largely on response quality and final outcomes rather than how support unfolds over time. We conduct a trajectory-centered evaluation of process fidelity across ten human, reconstructed, and synthetic counseling datasets. Our results show that synthetic dialogues often reach plausible endpoints but differ from human support in recovery dynamics and turn-by-turn responsiveness. While generation design can shift global properties such as recovery timing and trajectory structure, contingent patient--counselor responsiveness remains consistently lower in fidelity across models and generation paradigms. Our experiments on controlled synthetic datasets show that targeted generation interventions can narrow the gap with real data on several trajectory-level measures, but do not fully recover interactional fidelity, with turn-level responsiveness remaining limited. We release three controlled synthetic datasets comprising 2,050 dialogues, together with annotations and the evaluation framework.

title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
text:
arXiv:2611.31687v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

title: GeoMVGen: Joint Appearance-Geometry Modeling for Multi-View Video Generation in Robotic Manipulation
text:
arXiv:2611.31689v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Robotic manipulation requires predicting how robot-object interactions evolve over time, encompassing both visual appearance and scene geometry. In multi-camera settings, such predictions need to capture the evolving 3D scene consistently across viewpoints, while supporting controllable generation under different robot actions and camera configurations. Existing video generation models provide strong priors for visual appearance and motion but typically lack explicit geometric modeling. Meanwhile, recent advances in geometry-aware and multi-view generation have explored joint appearance-geometry modeling and cross-view consistency, yet generating temporally coherent appearance and geometry across multiple viewpoints under robotic manipulation conditions remains challenging. In this work, we propose GeoMVGen, a framework for joint multi-view RGB and pointmap video generation in robotic manipulation. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework employs modality-specific adaptation modules to capture the distinct characteristics of appearance and geometry, while using cross-modal residual connections to facilitate information exchange between the two modalities. To establish geometric correspondences across viewpoints, we further introduce a cross-view projection mechanism with complementary geometric supervisions, combining pointmap consistency with geometry foundation model-guided feature alignment. These designs enable controllable generation of temporally evolving multi-view observations with coherent appearance and geometrically consistent scene structures. Extensive experiments on 4D video generation dataset comprising simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios demonstrate that GeoMVGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods in video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency.

title: GRUN: Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network for Image Restoration
text:
arXiv:2611.31690v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Image restoration remains a fundamental challenge in low-level vision, requiring methods that handle diverse degradations while preserving scene structures and details. We revisit classical Retinex theory and propose a Generalized Retinex formulation that extends the illumination-reflectance decomposition into a Retinex-inspired content-environment factorization prior for image restoration. The key idea is to restore images using two learned factors: a content-dominant response (generalized reflectance) capturing scene properties and an environment-side response (generalized illumination) encoding task-dependent variations associated with the observed degradations. Based on this formulation, we develop GRUN (Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network), a MAP-guided deep unfolding framework that alternates reflectance restoration, illumination estimation, and progressive degradation inference across K stages with degradation-conditioned proximal operators. We further introduce a Degradation-aware Coupling Regularizer (DCR) that combines mutual information minimization, gradient decorrelation, and scale anchoring to promote complementary content-environment factor representations. Experiments on seven image restoration tasks, including denoising, dehazing, deraining, low-light enhancement, deblurring, underwater enhancement, and backlit enhancement, demonstrate competitive results on multiple benchmarks using the same architecture with task-specific weights. Moreover, the proposed Generalized Retinex design can be integrated into existing restoration methods, demonstrating its cross-architecture applicability. Code will be released.

title: E-Waste-Bench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Visual Triage of Data-Center Hardware
text:
arXiv:2611.31703v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Retired data-center hardware can often be refurbished or resold, but triage demands more than object categories. A model must tell visually similar parts apart, judge condition under damage and occlusion, and read the printed part number. We audit nine public e-waste collections. They cover mostly consumer devices (only 10% of images are labeled as a data-center part), label neither condition nor printed text, and contain 42% exact or augmented duplicates. We introduce E-Waste-Bench, 328K photographs drawn from 762K deduplicated images and labeled for class (24 classes), granularity, condition and printed text. Images come from those collections and the web, where a recipe-based crawler works beside an agent built on an open-weight vision-language model. The agent vets new sources and reads sites the crawler cannot parse, and both are steered toward under-represented classes. Training labels are model-made, splits follow near-duplicate groups, and human annotators label a test set of nearly 10,000 images. We benchmark classification, condition, detection, text perception and cross-dataset transfer. On this test set, a ConvNeXt-T trained on E-Waste-Bench reaches 64.3% top-1, against 31.5% with the public collections alone. Near-duplicate leakage inflates top-1 by 3.0 points under model-made test labels but by less than 0.1 under human labels, so model-labeled benchmarks need group splits. Accuracy falls to 42.1% on marketplace and auction photographs, the closest proxy for hardware leaving service. Data and code will be released.

title: PRETZEL: A Benchmark for Cyclic Peptide Structure Prediction
text:
arXiv:2611.31708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are a growing therapeutic modality, and co-folding models are increasingly used to predict their structures. Yet published evaluations rely on small, loosely curated target sets that differ from paper to paper, so results are not comparable, and most report pose RMSD alone, without checking whether the predicted molecule is chemically correct. We introduce PRETZEL (Prediction of Ring-Enclosed Topology: Zero-shot Evaluation of cycLic peptides), a benchmark of 285 curated cyclic peptide-protein complexes spanning three cyclization chemistries, all post-dating the training cutoff of every model evaluated. PRETZEL has three components: PRETZEL-SET, an evaluation set annotated by cyclization chemistry and chemical novelty; PRETZEL-TWIST, a specification layer that compiles a single canonical macrocycle description into each engine's native input format and verifies the returned structure; and PRETZEL-SALT, an evaluation suite pairing standard pose metrics with validity checks for bond distances, bond angles, dihedrals, and ring closure. Using these, we evaluate AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Protenix-v2, and HighFold3. Protenix-v2 achieves the best median RMSD at 9.05 A, with 19.3% of predictions under 2 A and 37.5% under 5 A. Accuracy varies by cyclization chemistry: models handle head-to-tail macrocycles relatively well but degrade on stapled targets. Chemical validity is weaker still: at most 8.1% of predictions have a fully valid set of inter-residue bonds, and no engine closes every macrocycle in more than 80.7% of its predictions, so pose accuracy alone is an insufficient criterion. These failures share a cause: co-folding models place macrocycles without representing them, treating cyclization and non-canonical chemistry as annotations layered onto a residue sequence rather than as first-class structure. PRETZEL is released with all inputs, predictions, and evaluation code.

title: NOBODY Was There: Bridging the Human-VLM Gap in Unwarranted Person Attribution Bias
text:
arXiv:2611.31714v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Describing an image requires not only recognizing what is visible but deciding what should be inferred. We investigate a systematic gap between humans and VLMs in their tendency to attribute visible actions or events to people who are not present in an image. We term this behavior unwarranted person attribution bias and find that, across 25 SOTA VLMs, captions of person-absent scenes mention a person four times as often as human-written captions of the same images. Through a preference study, we further show that both humans and VLMs prefer captions that avoid such attributions. Motivated by this, we introduce NOBODY, a preference dataset designed to bridge the gap between humans and VLMs in unwarranted person attribution. Through direct preference optimization (DPO), we align open VLMs on NOBODY and show that their agreement with human captions on person attribution reaches or exceeds inter-human agreement, whereas nine existing public preference datasets leave this behavior largely unchanged. Furthermore, we show that human judges preferred the aligned VLM captions significantly more than those of the baseline model. Alongside NOBODY, we release NOBODY-Bench, which evaluates VLMs for unwarranted person attribution bias and their alignment against human captions and preference. Project page: https://pmadinei.github.io/NOBODY/

title: EventSSM: Causal Spatial-State Modelling for Asynchronous Events Event-Depth Estimation
text:
arXiv:2611.31720v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Event cameras report asynchronous brightness changes, yet metric-depth supervision is typically available only at sparsely sampled reference timestamps. Aggregating events into frame-like representations simplifies learning but can obscure the fine-grained temporal structure of the original event stream. We introduce EventSSM, a causal spatial-state framework for event-associated metric-depth estimation using a recurrent memory updated by chronological event packets. To bridge asynchronous predictions and frame-time supervision, predicted event depths are geometrically transported using calibrated camera poses and differentiably rendered at reference timestamps. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate improvements over established event-depth methods across multiple depth-error measures. Controlled ablations further examine cross-modal initialization, temporal recurrence, individual state, readout, and supervision components, and packet subdivision. Together, these findings establish EventSSM as an effective framework for causal event-associated metric-depth estimation, combining persistent spatial context with physically timed state retention.

title: fork() for Agents: Agent Kernel for Non-blocking LLM Orchestration
text:
arXiv:2611.31727v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and recent agent runtimes (Sherlock, AgentGit, Atomix) preserve completed work through verifiers, version control, or transactional tool boundaries. We present \textbf{Agent-Kernel}, a non-blocking runtime that ports this pattern to the LLM \emph{content plane}: its primitive, \textbf{Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR)}, fires on a raw exception with no trained verifier or planner, resets a failed node's descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes each parent's text into its children's prompts (context inheritance), all on a durable substrate with a formal state-preservation guarantee. Across 14{,}434 runs on synthetic and standard benchmarks (tau-bench, Gaia2, AutomationBench, InterruptBench), SGR reaches full recovery within budget=3 where whole-trajectory replay exhausts (100\% vs.\ 55\%), and is roughly 10$\times$ faster than an adapted Sherlock rollback that also recovers. It matches ReAct-serial accuracy within noise on linear workloads while adding recovery and parallelism (up to 12.7$\times$ speedup) where structure permits. Ablation isolates SGR: removing it collapses success to 39.4\%.

title: Tokenization and Architecture Jointly Allocate Component Roles in Time Series Transformers
text:
arXiv:2611.31730v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. We propose a temporal probing framework that uses 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability of temporal properties from one sub-layer to the next (a matched MLP probe already saturates at the embedding). It targets models whose probed representations are read by a linear forecasting head. Applied to 5 supervised models trained on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks, it finds that the constructing component is not fixed but allocated by the interaction of tokenization and architecture. Under patch tokenization (PatchTST), the FFN's gain exceeds attention's in probing on all 8 datasets, and its 8-dataset mean is 3.2x attention's. Without attention, the FFN alone reaches nearly the same total gain, both when attention is removed from a trained model and when PatchTST is trained without it, and the retrained model forecasts within a few percent of the full model. In probing, attention dominates under variate tokenization (iTransformer); in CATS, cross-attention is the only input path. In a controlled manipulation of PatchTST, single-scalar tokens (P=1) nearly eliminate the FFN's construction, while one more point per token (P=2) restores it. Our forecasting-side interventions (activation patching, knockout, and training without attention) establish component-level reliance and sufficiency. These results offer a representational reading of prior findings on the gains from patching, the competitiveness of self-attention-free models (TSMixer, PatchMLP), and the distinct role of cross-attention in CATS.

title: Geo-SMILE: Statistical Model-Agnostic Interpretability with Local Explanations for Geospatial Machine Learning
text:
arXiv:2611.31731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conventional post-hoc explanation methods were developed largely for non-spatial inputs and often provide limited explicit treatment of geographic context. We introduce Geo-SMILE, a model-agnostic framework that distinguishes substantive Feature explanation from geographic-position response through complementary perturbation branches. The Feature branch masks substantive predictors while retaining observed coordinates; the Geo branch relocates geographic units while holding substantive predictors fixed. Following the statistical-distance-weighted surrogate principle of SMILE, input-distribution Wasserstein distances determine coalition locality weights and weighted Ridge surrogates approximate expected black-box predictions. GeoSensitivity, signed in the keep orientation, quantifies fitted-model responses to geographic-player relocation under the specified design. Across crime prediction in Hull, housing-price prediction in Seattle and ride-hailing demand in Chicago, held-out weighted surrogate fidelity ranges from $R_w^2=0.910$ to $0.989$ in the Feature branch and from $0.842$ to $0.906$ in the Geo branch. The framework makes geographic position an explicit object of post-hoc explanation while requiring separate assessment of interpretation, stability and reference dependence.

title: BEARING: Who Is Talking to Whom? Grounding Acoustic Direction in Vision for Online Multi-Party Conversation
text:
arXiv:2611.31735v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding a group conversation means deciding, from video and audio, who is speaking and to whom. Leading systems treat these tasks offline on single-channel clips and align models with a self-evaluation reward. We propose BEARING, a geometry-first alternative built on one measured signal: the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound. A label-free calibration learned from the stream registers this direction into the camera image, and an online registry of faces, voices and directions needs no enrollment. The registered direction serves as (i) a visual prompt for a vision-language model, a marker on the speaker or an arrow toward an off-screen source; (ii) one input of a reliability-weighted fusion with visual active-speaker detection, for speakers in the same direction from the array; and (iii) a verifiable reward for alignment: the named speaker must sit where the sound comes from, the confidence must match that check, and always answering "group" earns nothing. Every decision is online, with the lookahead as an explicit parameter. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from three AMI sites and egocentric EasyCom, the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%; addressee accuracy moves by about two points, because telling one addressee from the group depends on the words more than on where people are. For co-located speakers on AVDIAR, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%. The verifiable reward beats self-evaluation under GRPO, reward-ranked fine-tuning and DPO; shrinking the lookahead from 5 s to 0.5 s costs 4.5 DER points on AMI, and learning the registration online costs a dip in the first two minutes before the system overtakes vision alone. Code and evaluation protocols will be released.

title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
text:
arXiv:2611.31736v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs.
  On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

title: GreenDynaMix: Thermal-Aware Dynamic Mixed-Precision MoE LLM Inference Systems
text:
arXiv:2611.31737v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.

title: LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models
text:
arXiv:2611.31740v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.

title: FN-Prune: Training-Free Expert Pruning with Finite RMSNorm Perturbations
text:
arXiv:2611.31747v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Expert pruning reduces the memory footprint of mixture-of-experts language models, but retaining model quality depends on which experts are removed.
